Fig. 3: Overview of our research. We downloaded our dataset in May–July 2025. We reached out to arXiv and to authors of “problematic”
submissions in August 2025. We will wait at least 90 days (in line with best practices [66]) before disseminating our findings.
the source files in their natural format. To handle the unzip-
ping / unpacking, we relied on 7zip [52], which is free and
supports both Windows and Linux OSes.
Focus on precision. The other dilemma we faced when
developing BaRDE was whether to opt for (a) coverage or
(b) precision. We could either develop a tool that, in cases of
uncertainty in determining the root file of a TEX project, may
have made a decision that could have raised “false positives”
(e.g., flagging residual data that is actually an integral part of
the TEX project); or favor a more conservative approach. We
favored precision: if BaRDE cannot determine the root file of
a TEX project, the submission is skipped (but a log is updated).
Importantly, BaRDE operates statically and does not carry
out TEX compilation at runtime, which is a computationally
demanding task (we validate this assertion in §5).
Workflow. We provide the generic pseudocode of BaRDE’s
workflow in Alg. 1 (extended by the functions in Alg. 2 in the
Appendix). BaRDE inspects all files in a given 𝑖𝑛𝑝𝑢𝑡_𝑓𝑜𝑙𝑑𝑒𝑟
and stores the results of its analysis in dedicated 𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑠: one for
PDF files, one for TEX projects, and another for files excluded
from the analysis. If a file is a PDF, BaRDE updates 𝑃𝐷𝐹_𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑡
and begins to inspect the next submission. If a file is a GZ
file, BaRDE unpacks it and analyzes its contents—which are
always a single file. Three cases can happen:
a) the file is a blob, i.e., a TEX project, for which it is necessary
to infer its TEX root and then infer its residual data (which
can span both residual files and textual comments);
b) the file is a valid TEX file (and, hence, the submission is
a project), implying that the only residual data of this
project are the potential comments included in this file;
c) the file is of an unrecognized type, or BaRDE cannot infer
the TEX root of a blob: the submission will be skipped.
While analyzing a (valid) TEX project, BaRDE stores the fol-
lowing information: the corresponding 𝑠𝑢𝑏𝑚𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛.𝐼𝐷: the
filenames and sizes of all of its 𝑢𝑠𝑒𝑑and of its 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑖𝑑𝑢𝑎𝑙files;
and all the comments found in each 𝑢𝑠𝑒𝑑TEX file.

Low-Level Heuristics for Analyzing TEX Projects. We
explain the ideas behind three functions of BaRDE, shown
Alg. 1: BaRDE pseudocode (extended in Algorithm 2)
Input: 𝑖𝑛𝑝𝑢𝑡_𝑓𝑜𝑙𝑑𝑒𝑟containing the submissions’ source files (GZ
and PDF) extracted from the chunks downloaded from S3.
Output: 𝑟𝑒𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑡containing, for each submission that is a valid TEX
project: statistics on its used & residual files, as well as the
concatenation of the textual comments found in its (used)
TEX files; and the submissions that have been excluded.
1 𝑃𝐷𝐹_𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑡,𝑇𝑒𝑋_𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑡,𝑒𝑥𝑐𝑙𝑢𝑑𝑒𝑑_𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑡←emptyList();
2 for submission in 𝑖𝑛𝑝𝑢𝑡_𝑓𝑜𝑙𝑑𝑒𝑟do
3
if submission.type = "PDF" then
4
𝑃𝐷𝐹_𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑡←𝑠𝑢𝑏𝑚𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛.𝐼𝐷;
5
continue
6
// If here, then it’s a GZ file, which must be unzipped
7
𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑡←unzip(𝑠𝑢𝑏𝑚𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛);
8
// 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑡always has only one file
9
if content.type = "TeX" then
10
𝑇𝑒𝑋_𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑡←singleTeX(𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑡,𝑠𝑢𝑏𝑚𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛.𝐼𝐷);
11
continue
12
if content.name = submission.ID then
13
// 𝑓𝑖𝑙𝑒is blob, which must be unpacked
14
𝑟𝑜𝑜𝑡,𝑢𝑛𝑝𝑎𝑐𝑘𝑒𝑑←inferRoot(𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑡);
15
if root = ∅then
16
𝑒𝑥𝑐𝑙𝑢𝑑𝑒𝑑_𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑡←𝑠𝑢𝑏𝑚𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛.𝐼𝐷;
17
continue
18
𝑇𝑒𝑋_𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑡←
multiTeX(𝑟𝑜𝑜𝑡,𝑢𝑛𝑝𝑎𝑐𝑘𝑒𝑑,𝑠𝑢𝑏𝑚𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛.𝐼𝐷);
19
continue
20
// Unrecognized file or withdrawn submission, skip
21
𝑒𝑥𝑐𝑙𝑢𝑑𝑒𝑑_𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑡←𝑠𝑢𝑏𝑚𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛.𝐼𝐷;
22 𝑟𝑒𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑡←𝑇𝑒𝑋_𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑡, 𝑃𝐷𝐹_𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑡,𝑒𝑥𝑐𝑙𝑢𝑑𝑒𝑑_𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑡;
23 return 𝑟𝑒𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑡
in Alg. 2 (in the Appendix B), which also provides addi-
tional low-level details on BaRDE: extractComments(𝑓𝑖𝑙𝑒),
inferRoot(𝑏𝑙𝑜𝑏), findResidual(𝑟𝑜𝑜𝑡,𝑢𝑛𝑝𝑎𝑐𝑘𝑒𝑑).
Extracting comments. To determine text classifiable as
“comment” in a TEX file, we inspected the content of such a
file and identified either: lines starting with %; or text con-
tained within \begin{comment} \end{comment}, iffalse fi,
or if0 fi, all of which being well-known methods to mark
text that will not be shown in the final PDF (used also in [42]).

Extracting comments. To determine text classifiable as
“comment” in a TEX file, we inspected the content of such a
file and identified either: lines starting with %; or text con-
tained within \begin{comment} \end{comment}, iffalse fi,
or if0 fi, all of which being well-known methods to mark
text that will not be shown in the final PDF (used also in [42]).
